title: Ex 8.16 · Product distributes over union
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $A \times (B \cup C) = (A \times B) \cup (A \times C)$. The elements of these sets are ordered pairs, so follow a pair $(x, y)$.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A × (B ∪ C)) or a statement about an ordered pair (x, y) (like x ∈ A and y ∈ B, or (x, y) ∈ A × B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: (x, y) ∈ A × (B ∪ C) means x ∈ A and y ∈ B ∪ C.
Unpack y ∈ B ∪ C, then distribute 'x ∈ A and' over the 'or'.
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) says (x, y) ∈ A × B, and (x ∈ A and y ∈ C) says (x, y) ∈ A × C.
solution: Let $(x, y)$ be any ordered pair. By the definition of $\times$, $(x, y) \in A \times (B \cup C)$ means $x \in A \land y \in B \cup C$, that is, $x \in A \land (y \in B \lor y \in C)$.
By the distributive law this is $(x \in A \land y \in B) \lor (x \in A \land y \in C)$.
That says $(x, y) \in A \times B$ or $(x, y) \in A \times C$, so $(x, y) \in (A \times B) \cup (A \times C)$.
Every step was an equivalence, so $A \times (B \cup C) = (A \times B) \cup (A \times C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the Cartesian product (Section 1.2) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

steps.content: x ∈ A and y ∈ B ∪ C
x ∈ A and (y ∈ B or y ∈ C)
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) or (x ∈ A and y ∈ C)
(x, y) ∈ A × B or (x, y) ∈ A × C

examples.name: x ∈ A attached to B only

steps.content: x ∈ A and (y ∈ B or y ∈ C)
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) or y ∈ C
